read.sections.0.text.note: Used the usual Indonesian name "Konvensi Perserikatan Bangsa-Bangsa tentang Hak-Hak Anak"; the simpler text says "PBB". Please check the wording of the two rights matches the official Indonesian text.
read.sections.0.text.back: Contributing means giving your time, skills, or help to make something better. Contributing doesn't have to be a big campaign, because everyday actions matter too. A learner can read with younger children, translate for people who have just arrived, keep a shared room clean, or join a club. These actions help people learn, feel accepted, and share in the work of a community. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child states that children have the right to express their opinions about things that affect them. The convention also states that children may join groups or form groups, and meet with other people.
read.sections.0.text.source: To contribute means to give your time, skills or help to make something better. Contributing does not have to mean a big campaign, because everyday actions matter too. A learner can read with a younger child, translate for someone who is new, keep a shared room clean or join a club. These actions help people learn, feel welcome and share the work of a community. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child says that children have the right to give their views on things that affect them. It also says that children can join or set up groups and meet with others.

read.sections.1.text.back: The learners at Hillside Learning Centre see rubbish near the bus stop in front of the building. They have three ideas. Idea 1, an angry post online, could make people upset and will not solve the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask the people who use the bus stop what is missing. People who are affected by a problem are called stakeholders (related parties). Here, stakeholders include the bus users, the learners, and the learning centre manager. Idea 3 turns that evidence into a short polite letter to the manager, with one clear suggestion, for example a new bin. Working together with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.
read.sections.1.text.source: Learners at Hillside Learning Centre noticed litter near the bus stop outside. They had three ideas. Idea 1, an angry post online, might upset people and would not fix the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask people who use the bus stop what is missing. People who are affected by a problem are called stakeholders. Here, the stakeholders include bus users, the learners and the centre manager. Idea 3 turns the evidence into a short, polite letter to the manager with one clear suggestion, such as a new bin. Working with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.

Idea 3 is a short polite letter to the manager. The letter asks for a new bin.

read.sections.2.text.back: A good contribution is safe. Before the clean-up, the learners talk with a teacher and get permission from the learning centre manager. They plan to wear gloves and use rubbish bags, and they arrange for the rubbish to be taken away. If they photograph the rubbish, the photo must not show anyone's face or personal information. You don't need to speak in public, post something online, or take risks to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who was involved? What will we do differently next time? Even a small change, like a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.
read.sections.2.text.note: Review: English "You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks" is a firm safety reassurance; "Kamu tidak perlu" is slightly softer. Consider "Kamu sama sekali tidak perlu ...". Also "Apa yang akan kita lakukan secara berbeda di lain waktu?" sounds a little translated.
read.sections.2.text.source: Good contributions are safe. Before a clean-up, the learners talk to a teacher and get permission from the centre manager. They plan to use gloves and bags, and they arrange for the rubbish to be taken away. If they take a photo of the litter, it should not show anyone's face or private information. You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who was included? What would we do differently next time? Even a small change, like a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: Helping must be safe. First, the learners talk with a teacher. The learning centre manager gives permission. They wear gloves and use rubbish bags. They plan where the rubbish is taken. Photos must not show people's faces. You don't need to speak in public or make a post online. After helping, look back. What changed? Who took part? What could be better next time?
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Helping must be safe. First, the learners talk to a teacher. The centre manager gives permission. They use gloves and bags. They plan where the rubbish goes. A photo must not show faces. You do not need to speak in public or post online. After you help, look back. What changed? Who was included? What can be better next time?

write.example.back: Our goal is to make the bus stop in front of our learning centre cleaner. First, we will find out what is missing. With a teacher, we will ask five bus users. We will ask the teacher and the learning centre manager for permission to hold a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs, and put the rubbish in bags so it can be taken away by the learning centre. We will not photograph people. After that, we will check the bus stop again and ask the users whether they see a change.
write.example.source: Our goal is to make the bus stop outside our centre cleaner. First, we will find out what is missing. With our teacher, we will ask five bus users. We will ask our teacher and the centre manager for permission to hold a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs and put the rubbish in bags for the centre to take away. We will not take photos of people. Afterwards, we will check the bus stop again and ask users if they see a change.

watch.summary.back: In this UNICEF video, young people give a message to world leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places they live. They ask the leaders to listen to young people and act. The video shows that young people have good ideas about problems that affect them. But ideas need to reach the right people. For this to work, young people need facts, help from adults, and a real chance to change things. You don't have to talk to world leaders to bring change. You can also help in small, safe ways, like reading with younger children or keeping a shared space clean.
watch.summary.source: In this UNICEF video, young people share messages for world leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places where they live. They ask leaders to listen to young people and to act. The video shows that young people have good ideas about problems that affect them. But ideas need to reach the right people. For this to work, young people need facts, help from adults and a real chance to change what happens. You do not have to speak to world leaders to make a difference. You can also help in small, safe ways, like reading with a younger child or keeping a shared space clean.
